verdicts.pending: guards an outcome any task runner shows: a case can carry it

cases.title: A task that adds a subdirectory of the task before it: a warm run leaves the cold run’s tree
A task that adds a subdirectory of the task before it: an unchanged tree replays all three
A task that adds a subdirectory of the task before it: editing the first keeps the second’s file and none of the first’s old bytes
cases.why: The second task’s entry holds only what it added; one that held the first task’s files restores their old bytes over the fresh build.

cases.title: A task that adds a subdirectory of the task before it: editing the second rebuilds its file beside the first’s
A task that adds a subdirectory of the task before it: undoing an edit to the second restores its first file
A task that declares the same tree of the task before it: a warm run leaves the cold run’s tree
A task that declares the same tree of the task before it: an unchanged tree replays all three
A task that declares the same tree of the task before it: editing the first keeps the second’s file and none of the first’s old bytes
cases.why: The second task’s entry holds only what it added; one that held the first task’s files restores their old bytes over the fresh build.

cases.title: A task that declares the same tree of the task before it: editing the second rebuilds its file beside the first’s
A task that declares the same tree of the task before it: undoing an edit to the second restores its first file
A file a later task deletes from an earlier task’s outputs stays deleted on warm runs
cases.why: A replay of the earlier task brings the file back; the later task must then remove it again, or its run must not be replayed.

cases.title: A later task’s same-length rewrite of an earlier task’s output survives warm runs, mtime pinned
cases.why: Judged by size and mtime alone, the rewrite looks like the earlier task’s file, and its old bytes win.

cases.title: A declared variable reaches the command
Changing a declared variable runs the task again
Going back to an earlier value restores that value’s outputs
An unset variable and an empty one are different values
`MODE` and `mode` are different variables
A variable the task does not declare changes nothing
A `.env` file at the workspace root does not set a task’s variable
cases.why: The run’s environment is the one the shell gave it: a file the task never declares reading sets a value no one passed, decided by where the runner happens to look.

cases.title: Neither `.env.local` nor the `.env.<NODE_ENV>` file sets a task’s variable
cases.why: The run’s environment is the one the shell gave it: a file the task never declares reading sets a value no one passed, decided by where the runner happens to look.

cases.title: A `.env` in the directory the run starts from does not set a task’s variable
cases.why: The run’s environment is the one the shell gave it: a file the task never declares reading sets a value no one passed, decided by where the runner happens to look.

cases.title: With a `.env` present, the value the shell sets is the one the task sees

cases.why: A runner that loads `.env` into a declared variable must key on it; one that does not load it is right too.

cases.title: A bin a project’s dependency ships is on that project’s task PATH
A dependency shipping a bin named `sh` does not become the shell that runs the command
cases.why: The task’s PATH decides what its command resolves, not which shell parses the command.

cases.title: A project under a directory holding `:` does not run a file the split PATH entry names relative to it
cases.why: Its `node_modules/.bin` joined into PATH splits in two at the `:`; the second half is relative, so it resolves against the task’s directory.

cases.title: Run from inside a project, its dependencies’ tasks still run first
Run from inside a project, a change in its dependency runs it again
A replay started from a project’s subdirectory restores each output at its own project
cases.why: Outputs belong to their project; the directory the run starts from changes none of their paths.

cases.title: A run from inside a project replays what a run from the root stored
Forwarded flags reach the command as written, never parsed and rewritten
cases.why: A runner that parses forwarded flags and writes them back merges repeats, re-cases names, and casts `0010` to `10`.

cases.title: An empty arg, spaces, a newline, quotes and `$HOME` each reach the command as one arg, unexpanded
Forwarded args that look like the runner’s own flags, and an inner `--`, reach the command
cases.why: Everything after the first `--` belongs to the task: the runner reads none of it.

cases.title: Forwarded args reach the requested task, not its dependency of the same task name
cases.why: The args were given for the task asked for; the dependency was not asked for, only pulled in.

cases.title: A project’s external dependency changing in the lockfile runs its task again
A change to an external dependency of a workspace package a project links runs that project’s task again
cases.why: What a project can import through a linked workspace is that workspace’s dependencies too.

cases.title: A lockfile change no part of a project’s dependencies holds replays its task
Installing again with nothing changed replays every task
Swapping which packages two dependency names install runs the task again
cases.why: The same packages are installed, but `foo` now resolves to the other one.

cases.title: Swapping which packages two of the root’s dependency names install runs a task reading them
cases.why: A project resolves the root’s dependencies too: they are installed where every project finds them.

cases.title: An edit inside a local directory dependency runs the task of the project depending on it
cases.why: The lockfile names only the directory’s path, so its content is what changed.

cases.title: An edit inside a local directory dependency replays the projects that do not depend on it
A file added to a local directory dependency runs the task of the project depending on it
An edit to a file a local directory dependency links to runs the task depending on it
cases.why: A symlink in the directory installs as the file it names: that file is the dependency’s content.

cases.title: A change in a local directory dependency’s own node_modules replays the task depending on it
cases.why: An install copies the directory without its node_modules: nothing the task reads changed.

cases.title: An edit inside a `link:` directory dependency runs the task of the project depending on it
A committed edit inside a local directory dependency selects the project depending on it
An edit to a local dependency kept inside another project’s directory runs the task of the project depending on it
A committed edit to a local dependency kept inside another project’s directory selects the project depending on it
cases.why: The edit is under `other`’s directory, but `lib` is the project that installs it.

cases.title: A committed edit beside a local dependency, in the project that holds it, selects only that project
A change to the dependencies of a workspace package linked under another name runs the linking project’s task again
cases.why: `"y": "link:../b"` installs b itself: what `a` imports through `y` is everything b reaches.

cases.title: A workspace package linked under another name is a dependency: its build runs first
cases.why: `"y": "link:../b"` installs the workspace b, as `"b": "workspace:*"` does.

cases.title: A dependency change of a workspace nested in another’s directory runs the nested project’s task again
A dependency change of a workspace nested in another’s directory replays the outer project’s task
An override that forces a different transitive dependency runs the task of the project reaching it
An override replays the task of a project that does not reach the overridden package
Respelling an override so it resolves the same package replays every task
A workspace package the root depends on builds before a project that reads it through the root
cases.why: The root installs it where every project resolves it, whatever that project’s own manifest says.

cases.title: A change to a workspace package the root depends on runs a project reading it through the root again
A package the root depends on that itself depends on another workspace forms no cycle
cases.why: util reaches lib through the root, but lib depends on util: an edge back would be a cycle no manifest wrote.

cases.title: A committed change to a workspace package the root depends on selects a project reading it through the root
A task with caching off runs on every run
Changing a task’s command runs it again
Changing a dependency’s command rebuilds the projects that read its output
Declaring a new output runs the task again so the cache holds it
cases.why: An entry saved before the output was declared does not hold it; a hit would restore a tree without it.

cases.title: Committing a change keeps the entry the uncommitted run saved
An edit that keeps a source’s length, right after a run, runs the task again
cases.why: Size and a coarse mtime can both match; only the bytes tell the edit apart.

cases.title: Writing a source again with the same bytes replays the task
cases.why: Only the mtime moved; the key is the content.

cases.title: Adding an empty file under the inputs runs the task again
cases.why: A file’s existence is input even with no bytes in it.

cases.title: Changing one byte in the middle of a binary input runs the task again
Changing the last byte of a 2 MB input runs the task again
A declared variable set to its own name is not the same as the variable unset
A task reading every project file replays though a sibling task wrote its gitignored output: ignored in the workspace’s .gitignore
cases.why: Git does not list the ignored output, so it is no input; reading it as one reruns the reader after every build.

A task that exits non-zero fails the run
A failed task is not replayed as a success next time
A failed dependency stops the projects that need it from running
Fixing a failed task’s input makes the next run pass and build

cases.title: SIGINT to the run reaches a running task as SIGINT
cases.why: A cleanup bound to one signal (Node’s process.on, a shell trap) runs only if that signal arrives; one forwarded as another skips it.

cases.title: SIGTERM to the run reaches a running task as SIGTERM
cases.why: A cleanup bound to one signal (Node’s process.on, a shell trap) runs only if that signal arrives; one forwarded as another skips it.

cases.title: A task that exits 0 on Ctrl-C does not start its dependants
cases.why: The user asked the run to stop; a task that handles the signal by exiting cleanly has not finished its work.

cases.title: Ctrl-C ends a run whose task ignores SIGINT and SIGTERM
cases.why: A task that shrugs the polite signal off must still die: the run neither hangs nor leaves it running.

cases.title: A run stopped by SIGTERM exits only once its tasks have
cases.why: A runner that exits while its tasks are still shutting down leaves them writing to the terminal, and to files, after the prompt is back.

cases.title: One Ctrl-C lets a task finish its cleanup
cases.why: A handler that runs once (process.once, a trap that resets itself) dies mid-cleanup if the task hears the stop twice.

cases.title: A process a task backgrounded gets to clean up on SIGTERM after the task’s shell has died
A task that traps Ctrl-C and exits 0 is not cached with its partial outputs
cases.why: Its exit 0 came from the stop, not the end of its work: cached, the partial tree replays as a success.

cases.title: A task that finished before Ctrl-C is replayed by the next run
A run started with SIGHUP ignored (nohup) runs on when the terminal closes
cases.why: `nohup` asks for exactly this; a runner that installs its own SIGHUP handler over the inherited ignore stops the run.

cases.title: A dependency killed by a signal mid-write leaves no dependant cached from its partial output
cases.why: The kill switch is no input, so a healthy run derives the same keys: anything cached from the partial tree replays as a green hit.

cases.title: A concurrency of 0 is refused or read as a limit, never a run that waits for good
A task past its time limit is killed, fails the run, and is not cached
A task that finishes inside its time limit succeeds
A timed-out task that traps SIGTERM and exits 0 still fails, and its partial output is not cached
cases.why: Its exit 0 is the graceful-shutdown pattern answering the kill, not finished work: cached, the partial output replays as a success.

cases.title: A timed-out task that ignores SIGTERM is killed anyway, and the run does not hang
A timeout kills what the task backgrounded, not only its shell
cases.why: `sh -c "server & wait"` left the server alive under init after every timeout.

cases.title: A timeout kills a backgrounded child that ignores SIGTERM after its shell has died
cases.why: The shell dies on SIGTERM; a kill escalation cleared on its exit leaves the child running (nx#11782).

cases.title: A time limit no timer can hold is refused, not turned into an instant kill
cases.why: A timer past its bound fires at once: a 317-year limit killed the task in milliseconds, the inverse of what was asked.

cases.title: A task that fails once and passes on its retry passes the run, and the passing attempt is what is cached
A task that fails every attempt runs once plus its retries, then fails the run
A task with retries that passes first time runs once
A task killed by a signal the run did not send is retried like any failure
cases.why: Only the user’s stop ends the retries; a task the OOM killer or its own script killed failed.

cases.title: Ctrl-C during a task with retries does not attempt it again
cases.why: The task failed because the user stopped the run; a retry restarts what they asked to end.

cases.title: A retry does not remove the output directory a task beside it is writing into
cases.why: The retry cleaned its failed attempt’s file and pruned the emptied directory a sibling had just made.

cases.title: A dev server starts after its dependencies’ builds and runs until Ctrl-C, which ends it
A task that needs a server runs while the server is up, and the run ends when the task does
cases.why: An e2e suite against a dev server is the reason to depend on one; killing the server when the dependant starts (nx#27986), or refusing the edge, leaves no way to say it.

cases.title: A run whose task fails beside a server fails promptly and stops the server
A server the run no longer needs is asked to stop politely, so its cleanup runs
cases.why: A server that is SIGKILLed outright cannot remove its lock file, flush its log or release its port cleanly.

cases.title: A server that ignores SIGTERM does not keep a finished run from exiting
A server’s own child that ignores SIGTERM does not keep a finished run from exiting
cases.why: `server & wait`: the shell dies on SIGTERM, the server it started ignores it and holds the output pipe (nx#8286).

cases.title: A server that exits non-zero as it starts fails the run instead of hanging it
A server whose shell exits leaves nothing it started holding its port
At a concurrency of 1 a server’s dependant still runs
cases.why: A server never exits: a scheduler that holds its one slot until it does never starts the task that needs it.

cases.title: At a concurrency of 1 the tasks behind a running server still run one at a time
cases.why: Once the server was up, its dependants ran together past the limit (nx#31494, nx#34117).

cases.title: A server that depends on another server starts after it, and both stay up while a task needs them
cases.why: An app’s dev server over a library’s watcher is the common shape; refusing the edge or starting the app without its upstream breaks it (turborepo#8484).

cases.title: Every server a run selects starts, at a concurrency below their count
cases.why: Servers never finish, so they cannot wait for a slot: some of a filter’s servers never started (turborepo#4107).

cases.why: Booting a dev server for a run that runs nothing against it costs its whole start-up time (X-59). The server declares it reads no files, so its dependant can be keyed.

cases.title: A server that dies mid-run keeps the tasks that need it from starting, and fails the run
cases.why: Built against a dead server, the dependant reads as a pass or fails for the wrong reason; the run must say the server died.

cases.title: Ctrl-C before a server’s turn leaves it unstarted
cases.why: A server spawned after the stop comes up after the teardown and holds the run open.

cases.title: SIGINT to the run reaches a running server as SIGINT
cases.why: A server’s shutdown hook bound to one signal runs only if that signal arrives (turborepo#444, #12652, nx#23585).

cases.title: SIGTERM to the run reaches a running server as SIGTERM
cases.why: A server’s shutdown hook bound to one signal runs only if that signal arrives (turborepo#444, #12652, nx#23585).

cases.title: Ctrl-C ends a server’s own child that traps every signal it can
cases.why: The child of a continuous task, trapping TERM, INT and HUP, outlived Ctrl-C (nx#33460, nx#32438).

cases.title: A task that needs a server starts only once the server prints its ready line
A server that exits non-zero before its ready line fails the run and starts no dependant
A server whose command does not exist fails the run at once, not after waiting for its ready line
A server-style task that finishes with exit 0 before its ready line lets its dependants run
cases.why: It did its work and ended cleanly: there is no server left to wait for, and nothing failed.

cases.title: Ctrl-C while a server is still starting ends it and starts none of its dependants
A server that prints its ready line as Ctrl-C stops it does not start its dependants
cases.why: The line came from its shutdown, after the user stopped the run.

cases.title: A server that never prints its ready line fails at its time limit, and is killed
cases.why: Alive but never ready, it would otherwise hold the run open for good.

cases.title: A server that is ready inside its time limit keeps running past it
cases.why: For a server the limit bounds the wait for its ready line, not its life.

cases.title: A never-ready server that ignores SIGTERM is killed at its time limit anyway
A never-ready server that exits 0 on its time limit’s SIGTERM still fails
A never-ready server’s backgrounded child that ignores SIGTERM dies with it at its time limit
cases.why: The shell exits on SIGTERM at once; its child would hold the port into the next run.

cases.title: A never-ready server’s SIGTERM cleanup runs to its end at the time limit
cases.why: A handler that runs once dies mid-cleanup if the server hears SIGTERM twice.

A change in a project nothing depends on selects only that project

A new file git does not track yet counts as a change

cases.title: A tag works as a base, as a branch does

cases.title: In a depth-1 merge checkout, the first parent as base selects what the merge brought in
